patients.summary: Administrative assistant with hypothyroidism after radioactive iodine for Graves' disease who joins in 2020 and over six years collects a run of autoimmune diagnoses at outside specialists: discoid lupus, lichen planus, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, primary biliary cholangitis, then central hypothyroidism that turns out to be a macroprolactinoma found in July 2026 and just started on cabergoline.

documents.title: New Patient Visit — Establish Care
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
45 y/o woman, new to the practice. Works as an administrative assistant; she wanted a doctor she could actually reach and liked the membership model.

Thyroid: Graves' in 2015, treated with radioactive iodine in 2016, hypothyroid since and on levothyroxine 125 mcg every morning. Has an endocrinologist she sees about once a year and plans to keep. Feels well on this dose. No palpitations, no heat or cold intolerance, energy fine.

Gyn: periods regular. Prior practice did a Pap/HPV co-test in 2019, normal. Mammogram 2019 normal.
GI: colonoscopy at 40 because of her father, normal.

PMH: as above. PSH: none.
Meds: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother with rheumatoid arthritis. Father had autoimmune hypothyroidism and died of colon cancer at 65. Sister with lupus (SLE).
SH: never smoker, does not drink, no drug use. Desk job with a fair amount of filing.

ROS: negative in full except as above.

Exam: well-appearing, NAD. BP and HR per vitals. HEENT unremarkable. Neck: no thyroid tissue palpable, no nodes. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Extremities without edema. Skin without rash. Neuro nonfocal. Mood and affect normal.

A/P
1. Hypothyroidism after RAI for Graves' — clinically euthyroid. TSH today. Continue 125 mcg. Endo stays involved.
2. Health maintenance — Pap current (due 2024). Mammogram ordered. Colonoscopy due 2025 given FH. HCV and HIV once today. Flu shot given. Tdap 2017, current.
3. Labs: CMP, CBC, lipids, TSH.

RTC one year for physical, sooner as needed. She has the practice cell number.

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up letter
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group — clinic letter
Date of service: 01/31/2022

Dear Doctor,

I saw Ms. Winslow today for her scheduled hypothyroidism review. She was treated with radioactive iodine for Graves' disease and has been well controlled on levothyroxine 125 mcg daily for several years.

Over the last two months she has felt progressively more tired, her skin is drier, and she is cold in rooms that feel comfortable to others. She is taking her levothyroxine correctly and her sleep has not changed. Weight is unchanged. Of note, your office started oral estradiol with cyclic progesterone about three months ago for menopausal symptoms, which she says have improved a great deal.

Medications: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily; estradiol 1 mg daily; micronized progesterone 200 mg days 1-12.
Allergies: none known.
Family history: mother with RA, father with autoimmune hypothyroidism, sister with SLE.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, administrative assistant.

Examination is unremarkable apart from a mildly slow pulse. No thyroid tissue palpable.

Results today:
  TSH 7.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)
  Free T4 0.7 ng/dL (0.8-1.8)
  Total T3 80 ng/dL (100-200)

Impression: She is under-replaced, and the timing fits the oral estrogen. Oral estradiol raises thyroxine-binding globulin, and a patient without her own thyroid reserve cannot compensate, so free hormone falls on an unchanged dose.

Recommendations:
1. Rather than chase this with a higher levothyroxine dose, I would suggest moving her to transdermal estradiol, which has little effect on binding proteins. She is agreeable. I will leave the hormone prescription with you.
2. Keep levothyroxine at 125 mcg.
3. Repeat TSH and free T4 in about 8 weeks after the switch. If still low we will increase the dose.
4. Routine follow-up here in a year.

Thank you for letting me share in her care.

Endocrinology

medications.sig: Apply 1 patch to lower abdomen twice weekly; rotate sites

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Read the endo letter from 1/31: TSH 7.2, FT4 low, attributed to oral estradiol raising TBG. Called Jill. Stopping estradiol 1 mg tablets, starting estradiol 0.05 mg/day patch twice weekly. Same progesterone schedule. Levothyroxine stays at 125. TSH/FT4 in 8 weeks, standing order in. She asked whether the tiredness will lift — told her it should over a few weeks once levels settle; call if not.

Shoulder exam brief today: no swelling or redness, sore with reaching overhead. Neck full ROM, no radicular symptoms.

She would rather go straight to orthopedics — her employer's plan covers it and a coworker had a good experience. Referral placed. medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with food as needed for shoulder pain, up to 3 weeks

documents.title: Orthopedics consultation
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY — OFFICE CONSULTATION
DOS 03/16/2022
Referring: primary care

CC: R shoulder pain x 3 mo.

HPI: 47 yo RHD F, admin asst, endo saw her about two months ago for fatigue/cold intolerance on her thyroid replacement. R shoulder pain for 3 months, aggravated by overhead reaching to file on high shelves at work. Denies trauma.

PMH: hypothyroid s/p RAI for Graves. PSH: none. Meds: levothyroxine, estradiol patch, progesterone. All: NKDA.
SH: never smoker, no EtOH.

EXAM R shoulder: TTP lateral shoulder. Neer +, Hawkins +. PROM full. AROM full but painful arc in abduction 60-120 deg. Strength 5/5 ER/IR/supraspinatus with pain on empty can. No erythema, warmth or swelling. NVI distally.

IMAGING: XR R shoulder 3V today — no bony abnormality.

IMPRESSION: R shoulder subacromial impingement syndrome.

PLAN:
- PT for scapular stabilization and cuff strengthening, 6-8 wks
- Naproxen 500 mg BID with food PRN, 2-3 wks max
- Activity modification at work (step stool, lower the heavy files)
- If not improving at 6-8 weeks, return for subacromial corticosteroid injection

Orthopaedic Surgery

documents.title: Office Visit — Facial Rash
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Rash on her cheeks and nose that has been there since sometime in the winter and flares every time she is in the sun — worse since the days got longer. Not itchy, a little tender. Tried hydrocortisone OTC without much change. No joint pain, no mouth sores, no fevers. Feels fine otherwise. Shoulder much better after PT.

Exam: scaly red plaques on both cheeks and the bridge of the nose, some with lighter centers. Rest of skin not examined in detail today.

A/P: Photosensitive facial rash. Not typical rosacea or seb derm to my eye and with the sister's lupus I want dermatology to see it and likely biopsy. Referral placed. Sunscreen SPF 50 and a hat in the meantime.

medications.sig: Apply a thin layer to facial plaques twice daily on weekdays; none on weekends

reports.text:
Specimen: skin, left cheek, 4 mm punch biopsy.
Microscopic: Interface dermatitis with vacuolar change at the dermoepidermal junction. A perivascular and periadnexal mononuclear infiltrate is present in the superficial and deep dermis. Follicular plugging is noted.
reports.conclusion: Interface dermatitis with perivascular and periadnexal mononuclear infiltrate, consistent with discoid (chronic cutaneous) lupus erythematosus in the appropriate clinical setting.

documents.title: Dermatology consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Dermatology — new patient consultation
Service date 8/1/2022, letter completed after pathology

Thank you for sending Ms. Winslow, a 47-year-old woman with hypothyroidism after RAI for Graves' disease, for a facial eruption.

She describes several months of facial rash that is clearly worse after sun. She has no joint pains, no oral ulcers, and no systemic symptoms.

Meds: levothyroxine, estradiol patch, progesterone. Allergies: none.

On examination there are sharply marginated red plaques over both malar cheeks and the nasal dorsum. Centers are hypopigmented with a hyperpigmented rim; several plaques carry adherent scale, and there is atrophy with early scarring. I found nothing similar elsewhere on full skin exam. No lymphadenopathy. Remainder of the exam unremarkable.

A 4 mm punch biopsy from the left cheek shows an interface dermatitis with a perivascular and periadnexal mononuclear infiltrate.

Assessment: Discoid lupus erythematosus, localized to the face. No clinical features of systemic lupus today; with her sister's SLE I have told her what to watch for.

Plan:
- Clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily on weekdays to active plaques, off at weekends; we discussed atrophy risk on the face and the reason for the pulsed schedule.
- Daily broad-spectrum SPF 50+, wide-brim hat, sun avoidance midday.
- Antimalarial therapy is the next step if lesions keep forming.
- Follow up here as needed or if new lesions.

Dermatology

documents.title: Question about the skin cream
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The dermatologist's letter says discoid lupus. Does that mean I have what my sister has? And she gave me a strong steroid ointment for my face, is that safe to use for a long time?

documents.title: RE: Question about the skin cream
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good questions. Discoid lupus is a skin-only form; it is related to lupus but most people with it never develop the whole-body kind your sister has. Your exam and history don't show signs of that, and we'll keep an eye out at your visits. The weekday-on, weekend-off schedule is exactly how dermatologists use the strong ointment on the face to keep it safe — stick to their plan and sunscreen every day.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly visit.

Interval: endo in January — TSH had drifted up on oral estrogen, switched to the patch, recheck in March normal. Ortho for right shoulder impingement in March, did PT, discharged in May; reaches overhead without pain now. Dermatology in August diagnosed discoid lupus on the face by biopsy — using clobetasol on weekdays, wearing sunscreen religiously, plaques flatter.

Vasomotor symptoms controlled on patch plus cyclic progesterone; monthly withdrawal bleeds, nothing irregular.

Meds: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily, estradiol 0.05 mg/day patch twice weekly, progesterone 200 mg nightly days 1-12, clobetasol 0.05% ointment to face weekdays.
NKDA.

Exam: vitals fine. Face with a few flat pink plaques on cheeks, faint scarring, no active scale. Neck no nodes. Heart regular, lungs clear. Abdomen soft. R shoulder full ROM, negative Hawkins. No edema. No joint swelling.

A/P
1. Hypothyroidism after RAI: TSH today.
2. Discoid lupus, face: per derm. No systemic features.
3. R shoulder impingement: resolved after PT. Off problem list.
4. Hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms: continue, revisit yearly.
5. HM: flu today. Mammogram ordered. Pap 2024. Colonoscopy 2025. Bivalent COVID booster at her pharmacy next month.

RTC 1 year.

events.reason: Itchy rash on wrists, trunk and ankles

medications.sig: Apply to itchy body lesions twice daily for up to 4 weeks at a time; not on the face

reports.text:
Specimen: skin, left volar wrist, 4 mm punch.
Microscopic: Compact hyperkeratosis with wedge-shaped hypergranulosis and irregular acanthosis. A dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugs the dermoepidermal junction with basal vacuolar change and scattered colloid bodies.
reports.conclusion: Lichenoid interface dermatitis consistent with lichen planus.

documents.title: Dermatology return visit
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Dermatology — follow-up letter
Date of visit: 03/21/2023

Dear colleague,

Ms. Winslow came back to us, this time not for her face (the discoid lupus is quiet on pulsed clobetasol and strict photoprotection) but for an itchy eruption of about six months. It began on both wrists and has spread to the trunk and ankles. The itch is intense. Nothing new in her soaps, lotions or medications.

Examination: numerous flat-topped, violaceous, polygonal papules across the extremities and trunk, several with a fine white lacy surface pattern. Inside the cheeks there are white reticular patches on the buccal mucosa, which she had not noticed. No lymph nodes enlarged.

Punch biopsy from the left wrist: hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction.

Assessment: Lichen planus, cutaneous and reticular oral involvement.

Plan:
- Triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily to body lesions, in 4-week runs.
- The oral lesions are asymptomatic; we will simply watch them. Dental checkups as usual.
- Continue clobetasol for the face as before.
- Return if not settling in 2-3 months.

With kind regards,
Dermatology

orders.reason: Inflammatory polyarthritis of hands and wrists

documents.title: Office Visit — Hand and Wrist Swelling
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: For about six months her hands are stiff every morning, takes well over an hour before she can type properly. Both hands and wrists puffy. Some evenings she runs a low-grade temperature. Down about 5 lb without trying (scale here agrees, 71.2 kg vs 73.5 in Sept). Mom has RA and she's "pretty sure this is that." No rash beyond her known skin issues, no mouth ulcers, no Raynaud's, no chest pain.

O: Vitals reviewed, afebrile now. Boggy swelling and tenderness over the MCPs and PIPs of both hands, wrists tender. No deformity, no nodules. Rest of joints unremarkable.

A: Symmetric inflammatory small-joint polyarthritis, high suspicion for RA with the family history.

P:
- ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP, ANA, CBC with diff, CMP today.
- Urgent rheumatology referral; staff to call for an expedited slot.

documents.title: Results call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called Jill. ESR 50, CRP 30 mg/L (3.0 mg/dL), RF positive, anti-CCP positive, ANA negative. CBC and CMP normal. Explained this fits rheumatoid arthritis and that rheum will confirm and start treatment. Front desk got her in with rheumatology 11/27. Results faxed ahead.

medications.sig: Take 1½ tablets (300 mg) by mouth daily with food
10 mg daily x 2 weeks, 7.5 mg daily x 2 weeks, 5 mg daily x 1 week, 2.5 mg daily x 1 week, then stop

reports.text: Bilateral hands, PA, oblique and lateral views. Periarticular osteopenia about the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. Small marginal erosions at the MCP joints. Joint spaces otherwise maintained. No fracture or subluxation. Soft tissue swelling over the MCP joints.
reports.conclusion: Periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions, consistent with inflammatory (rheumatoid) arthritis.

documents.title: Rheumatology consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
RHEUMATOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: November 27, 2023

Reason for referral: inflammatory arthritis.

History: 49-year-old woman with hypothyroidism after RAI for Graves' disease and dermatology-diagnosed discoid lupus and lichen planus. She describes six months of morning stiffness lasting more than an hour that loosens with use, swelling of both hands and wrists, intermittent low-grade fevers and an unplanned 5-pound weight loss over the last few months.

Medications: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily, estradiol patch, cyclic progesterone, topical clobetasol and triamcinolone.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: mother RA; father autoimmune hypothyroidism; sister SLE.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, administrative assistant.

Examination: soft-tissue swelling with tenderness across the MCP and PIP joints of both hands. No deformity. Remaining joints normal.

Data (drawn by referring office 11/6): ESR 50 mm/hr; CRP 3.0 mg/dL; RF positive; anti-CCP positive; ANA negative.
Hand radiographs today: periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions.

Assessment: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, already erosive. The negative ANA is reassuring that the joint disease is not a lupus arthropathy, and her discoid lupus remains skin-limited.

Plan:
1. Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily; it also treats her discoid lupus. Baseline retinal exam within the year.
2. Prednisone taper starting at 10 mg to bridge symptoms over 6 weeks.
3. If she has not responded adequately at follow-up, add a second agent.
4. Return in 3 months with ESR and CRP.

Rheumatology

documents.title: Rheum letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Rheum letter in: seropositive erosive RA, started hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily and a prednisone taper from 10 mg. Med list updated. They want a baseline retinal exam — ophthalmology referral placed. Called Jill: tolerating both, stiffness already better on the prednisone. Reviewed taper schedule with her.

documents.title: Ophthalmology — baseline hydroxychloroquine exam
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Eye clinic report, exam 1/10/2024
Indication: baseline exam, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily started 11/2023 for RA.

VA cc 20/20 OD, 20/20 OS. Pupils equal and reactive, no afferent defect. IOP normal both eyes. Anterior segment quiet. Dilated fundus: healthy optic nerves, flat maculae with normal foveal reflex, normal vessels and periphery OU.
SD-OCT macula: normal foveal contour, intact ellipsoid zone both eyes.
Humphrey 10-2: reliable, full both eyes.

Impression: normal baseline exam, no retinopathy.
Plan: annual screening can begin after 5 years of use given her dose and normal kidney function, sooner if risk factors change.

Ophthalmology

documents.title: Rheumatology follow-up
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
Rheumatology clinic — follow-up note, 03/04/2024

RA, seropositive, erosive. On hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily since late November, prednisone taper finished in January.

She is much improved. Morning stiffness about 15 minutes, no swelling she can see, back to typing all day. No fevers. Weight stable.

Exam: no synovitis in hands, wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees or feet. Full fist both hands.

ESR 18 mm/hr, CRP 0.6 mg/dL today.

Assessment: good response to hydroxychloroquine monotherapy. Baseline eye exam in January was normal.
Plan: continue hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily. We will not add a second agent while she stays in this range. Recheck here in 6-12 months, sooner with any flare.

Rheumatology

documents.title: Office Visit — Pruritus and Jaundice
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Booked herself in after a coworker told her she looked yellow. Itching since roughly May, all over, much worse at night — up scratching, sleeping badly. Tried cetirizine and diphenhydramine from the drugstore with no effect. Over the last two months she has noticed her skin and the whites of her eyes yellowing. Tired for months, which she had put down to work. No abdominal pain, no fevers, no change in stool color she has noticed. No alcohol ever. No new meds or supplements; skin creams are her usual ones. No travel.

Meds: levothyroxine 125 mcg, estradiol patch 0.05 twice weekly, progesterone 200 mg days 1-12, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily, topical clobetasol and triamcinolone PRN.

O: Afebrile, vitals normal. Clearly icteric skin and sclerae. Excoriations on forearms and shins. Abdomen soft, nontender, liver edge palpable below the right costal margin, no spleen felt, no ascites. No asterixis.

A: Jaundice with pruritus, presumably cholestatic. Long list of autoimmune disease in her and her family puts PBC high on the list; obstruction has to be excluded.

P:
- Hepatic panel, INR, CBC, BMP now (stat to the lab).
- RUQ ultrasound.
- Urgent GI referral.
- Will call her tonight or tomorrow with results.

documents.title: Results — liver tests
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called patient with yesterday's results. Total bili 2.8, direct 1.5, alk phos 420, AST 80, ALT 75 — cholestatic pattern. INR 1.0. CBC and BMP fine. Added AMA; she'll come in tomorrow morning for the draw. Ultrasound scheduled 11/12. GI has her 11/18 — told her to call us if she gets abdominal pain, fever, confusion or dark tarry stool before then.

documents.title: AMA positive
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Antimitochondrial antibody positive. With the cholestatic panel this points strongly to primary biliary cholangitis. Forwarded to GI ahead of 11/18 visit. Portal message to patient: the antibody test supports the diagnosis we talked about; GI will go over treatment next week.

reports.text:
Indication: jaundice, cholestatic liver tests.
Liver: enlarged, 19 cm in craniocaudal length, with normal homogeneous echotexture and smooth contour. No focal lesion. Hepatic and portal veins patent with normal flow direction.
Biliary: no intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Common bile duct 4 mm. Gallbladder normally distended without stones, sludge or wall thickening. Sonographic Murphy sign negative.
Pancreas: visualized portions unremarkable.
Spleen: normal size.
No ascites.
reports.conclusion: Hepatomegaly with normal echotexture. No biliary dilatation or gallstones. No ascites.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Gastroenterology & Hepatology — Consultation
Visit 11/18/2024

Thank you for the urgent referral of Ms. Winslow, 50, who carries a history of Graves' disease treated with radioactive iodine, hypothyroidism, discoid lupus, lichen planus and rheumatoid arthritis.

For about six months she has been tired and itchy, the itch worst at night and not touched by over-the-counter antihistamines. For two months her skin has been turning yellow.

Medications: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily, estradiol patch with cyclic progesterone, topical steroids.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: no alcohol history of any kind; no recent travel; no high-risk sexual exposures. Never smoker.
Family: mother RA, father hypothyroidism and colon cancer, sister SLE.

Examination: afebrile, vital signs normal. Skin and sclerae icteric. Liver enlarged to palpation; no splenomegaly, no ascites. Murphy's sign negative.

Data reviewed from your office:
  Total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, direct 1.5 mg/dL
  Alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L (40-120)
  AST 80 U/L (10-40), ALT 75 U/L (7-56)
  INR 1.0
  Antimitochondrial antibody: positive
  RUQ ultrasound 11/12: hepatomegaly, normal echotexture, no ductal dilatation, no stones

Impression: Primary biliary cholangitis. A cholestatic profile, positive AMA and a non-obstructed biliary tree make the diagnosis without a biopsy. Hydroxychloroquine is not a convincing culprit for this pattern.

Plan:
1. Ursodiol 500 mg twice daily (about 14 mg/kg/day).
2. Cholestyramine 4 g daily for the itch. She must separate it by at least 4 hours from levothyroxine and ursodiol — reviewed a schedule with her (levothyroxine on waking, ursodiol with breakfast and dinner, cholestyramine mid-afternoon).
3. I would stop systemic hormone therapy while she is jaundiced; I will leave that with you.
4. Liver panel in 3 months, then follow-up here.
5. Baseline DXA — PBC carries bone-loss risk.
6. Confirm hepatitis A/B immunity and vaccinate as needed.

With thanks,
Gastroenterology

documents.title: Office Visit — Fatigue and Weight Gain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Since about April she's felt like she's moving through mud. Exhausted by mid-afternoon, cold all the time even in July, constipated for the first time in her life, cramps in her calves at night, and she says her thinking at work is sluggish — losing track of what she was doing. Up about 13 lb without eating differently. Periods have gone light and irregular since spring. Taking levothyroxine 125 every morning, nothing near it; ursodiol twice daily. No cholestyramine since February. No itching. Mood OK, just tired.

O: Pulse low 60s, BP normal. Weight 78.6 kg. Skin dry. Not icteric. No thyroid tissue. Heart slow-regular. Lungs clear. No edema.

PHQ-9: 4.

A: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation — reads like under-replacement, but she has been stable on this dose. Perimenopausal transition also in the mix for the cycles.

P:
- BMP, TSH, CBC, hepatic panel today.
- Results to her this afternoon.

Addendum 17:30: Na 132 (mild hyponatremia), rest of BMP normal. TSH 1.4 — normal. CBC normal. ALP 165, bili 0.8, still coming down. TSH doesn't explain how she feels; with her RAI history I'd like endo to look. Referral placed back to her endocrinologist; asked them to see her this month. Called and explained.

Endocrinology — clinic note
Seen 7/31/2025, referred back by primary care

Ms. Winslow, 50, with Graves' disease treated by radioactive iodine and hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 125 mcg daily. I last saw her in 2022 for fatigue and cold intolerance, which settled after her estrogen was moved to a patch. She has since been diagnosed with discoid lupus, lichen planus, RA and PBC.

Over four months: progressive fatigue, cold intolerance and a 6-kg weight gain. New constipation, muscle cramps, and what she calls sluggish thinking at work. Menses scant and irregular. No neck pain.

Medications: levothyroxine 125 mcg daily, ursodiol 500 mg twice daily, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily, topical steroids.
Allergies: NKDA.

BP 110/70, HR 58.
Skin cool and dry. Ankle jerks show delayed relaxation. Thyroid not palpable, not tender. Visual fields by confrontation in clinic: bitemporal peripheral loss.

Primary care's BMP of 7/14 is normal except mild hyponatremia (Na 132). TSH there 1.4.

Thyroid function drawn today; I will write again with results and a plan.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Endocrinology results letter
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology — results and plan, 8/4/2025

Dear Doctor,

Thyroid tests from 7/31: TSH 1.2 mIU/L, free T4 0.6 ng/dL (0.8-1.8).

Free T4 is low and the TSH is not raised to meet it. In someone with no meaningful thyroid of her own after RAI, that is the picture of central hypothyroidism: the pituitary is no longer driving the TSH response, and the TSH you checked on 7/14 was falsely reassuring. From here on her dose should be adjusted to free T4, not TSH.

Plan:
1. Levothyroxine increased to 137 mcg daily. New prescription sent.
2. Free T4 (with TSH for completeness) in 6 weeks; she can have it drawn at her physical in September.
3. Follow-up here in about a year.

I have explained to her that the dose change should help the fatigue and cold intolerance over several weeks.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Office Visit — Headaches and Visual Difficulty
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Two problems that she now thinks go together. (1) Dull, pressure-like headaches, frontal, that have been getting steadily worse over the past few months. (2) She keeps bumping into things — walked into a door frame at work last week, catches her hip on furniture at home. Says things "come out of nowhere" from the sides. Also: no period for about a year now. No hot flashes or sweats.

Meds: levothyroxine 137 mcg, ursodiol 500 mg BID, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily, topical steroids PRN.
NKDA.

O: BP and pulse normal, afebrile. Alert, appropriate. Acuity grossly normal with near card both eyes. Confrontation fields: reduced in the temporal fields of both eyes. Pupils equal and reactive. Fundi difficult undilated; discs look sharp where seen. EOMs full. Face symmetric. Strength, sensation, reflexes, gait normal. Neck supple.

A: Progressive headaches with bilateral temporal field loss and a year of amenorrhea in a woman with central hypothyroidism. Needs urgent imaging of the brain and sella.

P:
- MRI brain with and without contrast, marked urgent; staff to get the earliest slot.
- Messaged her endocrinologist; her overdue follow-up there will be moved up.
- Return or ED for sudden severe headache, double vision or sudden vision loss.

reports.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
reports.text:
Indication: progressive headaches, bitemporal visual field loss, amenorrhea.
Technique: multiplanar multisequence MRI of the brain before and after IV gadolinium, with thin-section coronal and sagittal imaging through the sella.
Findings: There is a 2.5 cm enhancing sellar and suprasellar mass, measured in craniocaudal dimension on coronal post-contrast images, extending upward from an expanded sella and compressing adjacent structures. The normal pituitary gland is not separately identified. No hemorrhage within the mass. The brain parenchyma is otherwise normal without mass effect elsewhere, hydrocephalus or abnormal enhancement. Ventricles normal in size. Major intracranial flow voids preserved.
reports.conclusion: 2.5 cm suprasellar mass compressing adjacent structures, most consistent with a pituitary macroadenoma. Endocrine correlation recommended.

documents.title: Endocrinology visit — pituitary mass
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology — clinic note, 7/20/2026

Ms. Winslow returns, brought forward after her primary care physician's MRI. History: Graves' disease treated with radioactive iodine about ten years ago, longstanding hypothyroidism, and central hypothyroidism diagnosed here last summer.

In her words, "I keep walking into furniture and door frames." She has dull, pressure-type headaches that have worsened over recent months. Her last menstrual period was about a year ago; before that she cycled regularly every 25-30 days, bleeding 3-4 days. She has had no hot flashes or night sweats.

Medications: levothyroxine 137 mcg daily, ursodiol 500 mg twice daily, hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: father died of colon cancer at 65.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, administrative assistant.

BP 130/78, HR 72, BMI 29 kg/m2.
Visual acuity 20/20 in each eye. Neurological examination otherwise normal. Breast examination: on palpation of the areola, milky discharge expressed bilaterally.

MRI 7/16 reviewed: 2.5 cm suprasellar mass compressing adjacent structures.

Impression: pituitary macroadenoma with galactorrhea and amenorrhea; a prolactinoma is the leading possibility. The bitemporal field loss needs formal measurement.

Plan:
- Prolactin (lab asked to run serial dilutions to avoid a hook effect), LH, FSH, free T4 today; 8 AM cortisol tomorrow morning.
- Formal visual fields with ophthalmology this month.
- I will call her with results and start treatment as indicated.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Endocrinology results letter — prolactinoma
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology — results and plan, 7/22/2026

Dear Doctor,

Results:
  Prolactin 2,140 ng/mL (after dilution)
  LH 1.1 mIU/mL, FSH 2.6 mIU/mL — inappropriately low for her age and amenorrhea
  Free T4 1.1 ng/dL on levothyroxine 137 mcg
  8 AM cortisol 13.6 mcg/dL — adequate; no steroid cover needed

A prolactin of this magnitude with a 2.5 cm sellar/suprasellar mass is diagnostic of a macroprolactinoma. It accounts for the galactorrhea and amenorrhea, the low gonadotropins, and in all likelihood the central hypothyroidism.

Treatment is medical first, even with field loss; dopamine agonists usually shrink these tumors and visual fields often improve within weeks.

Plan:
1. Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly, increasing to 0.5 mg twice weekly in two weeks if tolerated. Take with food at bedtime to limit nausea and lightheadedness.
2. Humphrey visual fields with ophthalmology 7/29.
3. Prolactin again in 4-5 weeks (order sent to your lab for convenience).
4. Repeat pituitary MRI in about 3 months.
5. Continue levothyroxine 137 mcg.
6. She should seek care immediately for sudden severe headache or sudden change in vision.

I spoke with her at length by phone this morning.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Ophthalmology — visual field assessment
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Neuro-ophthalmic assessment, 7/29/2026
Referred by endocrinology: 2.5 cm pituitary macroadenoma (prolactinoma), cabergoline started 7/22.

VA 20/20 OD, 20/20 OS. Pupils equal, no RAPD. Color vision full both eyes. IOP normal. Anterior segments quiet.
Dilated exam: optic discs pink and well-perfused without pallor, healthy rims. Maculae normal. No hydroxychloroquine changes.
Humphrey 24-2 SITA: reliable both eyes. Dense temporal hemifield defects in each eye respecting the vertical meridian — bitemporal hemianopia.

Impression: bitemporal hemianopia, in keeping with the known pituitary macroadenoma. No optic atrophy.
Plan: repeat fields in 6-8 weeks on cabergoline. Same-day contact for any sudden vision change.

Ophthalmology
